intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by biallelic mutation in the CCDC9 gene on chromosome 19q13.32.

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by biallelic mutation in the CCDC9 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a novel homozygous variant in CCDC9 (NC_000019.9: g.47763960C>T, NM_015603.3, NP_056418.1: p. Ser109Leu) in a patient from a consanguineous family.
checks.explanation: Paper reports a homozygous variant in one patient and calls CCDC9 a candidate/possible pathogenic gene; it does not name SPGF104 or establish causation firmly.

checks.claim: The CCDC9 gene is located on chromosome 19q13.32.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature; RefSeq accession indicates chromosome 19.

paragraphs.text: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is a form of male infertility. Sha et al. (2019) reported it as severe asthenozoospermia, with abnormal morphology and ultrastructure of the spermatozoa.

checks.evidence_quote: severe asthenozoospermia is a serious threat to the male reproductive health.

checks.claim: Sha et al. (2019) reported SPGF104 as severe asthenozoospermia with abnormal morphology and ultrastructure of the spermatozoa.

checks.explanation: Severe asthenozoospermia with damaged sperm morphology/ultrastructure is reported; the SPGF104 designation is not in the paper.

paragraphs.text: Khan et al. (2025) studied 7 large Pakistani families with male infertility, 5 of which were consanguineous. One of these families had male infertility and carried biallelic CCDC9 variants. The abstract did not give further clinical details on the affected men in this family.

checks.evidence_quote: We recruited seven large families with clinically diagnosed male infertility from rural Pakistan, including five with a history of consanguinity.

checks.evidence_quote: We recruited seven large families with clinically diagnosed male infertility from rural Pakistan, including five with a history of consanguinity.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of SPGF104 is autosomal recessive. Sha et al. (2019) found a homozygous CCDC9 variant in a man from a consanguineous family, and Khan et al. (2025) found biallelic CCDC9 variants in a Pakistani family.

checks.explanation: Autosomal recessive inheritance is implied by homozygosity in a consanguineous family but not stated.

paragraphs.text: In a man from a consanguineous family who had severe asthenozoospermia, Sha et al. (2019) identified a homozygous missense variant in the CCDC9 gene (NC_000019.9: g.47763960C-T; NM_015603.3), which resulted in a ser109-to-leu (S109L) substitution. In silico analysis predicted the variant to be highly pathogenic. The patient's spermatozoa had significantly reduced CCDC9 protein, along with severely damaged morphology and ultrastructure. Sha et al. (2019) concluded that CCDC9 may be a novel pathogenic gene for severe asthenozoospermia (see allelic variant SER109LEU).

checks.evidence_quote: we identified a novel homozygous variant in CCDC9 (NC_000019.9: g.47763960C>T, NM_015603.3, NP_056418.1: p. Ser109Leu) in a patient from a consanguineous family.
checks.explanation: Ser109Leu is a missense change; stated.

checks.claim: The CCDC9 variant identified by Sha et al. (2019) is NC_000019.9:g.47763960C-T (NM_015603.3), resulting in a ser109-to-leu (S109L) substitution.

checks.evidence_quote: The variant was highly pathogenic and was predicted to be a candidate gene for asthenozoospermia through in silico analysis.

paragraphs.text: Khan et al. (2025) performed whole-genome sequencing on 26 individuals from 7 large Pakistani families with male infertility. They identified plausible genetic causes in 5 of the 7 families (71%), compared with the 20% yield they had previously obtained from whole-exome sequencing of unrelated singleton cases. In 1 family, they found biallelic missense substitutions in CCDC9, which they described as a gene with emerging relevance to male infertility. The abstract did not specify the variants.

checks.evidence_quote: The rate of genetic findings using the current approach (71%) was much higher than what we recently achieved using whole-exome sequencing (WES) of unrelated singleton cases (20%).
checks.explanation: Plausible causes were found in five of the seven families, a 71% yield.
